```{r}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
```

All three datasets come from [Movebank](https://www.movebank.org/), the public
repository for animal tracking data, and are redistributed here under their
original licences for teaching. They live in the `data/` folder of the course
repository, gzipped — R reads `.csv.gz` directly, no need to decompress.

They were chosen because they **fail in different ways**. Real tracking data
is never clean, and each of these teaches a different lesson about that.

## Overview

```{r}
#| echo: false
files <- c(
  "African buffalo"  = "data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz",
  "Parti-coloured bat" = "data/bat_safi.csv.gz",
  "Turkey vulture"   = "data/vulture_leo.csv.gz"
)

summarise_track <- function(path) {
  d <- read.csv(path)
  ts <- as.POSIXct(d$timestamp, tz = "UTC")
  data.frame(
    Species     = unique(d$individual.taxon.canonical.name)[1],
    Sensor      = paste(unique(d$sensor.type), collapse = ", "),
    Individuals = length(unique(d$individual.local.identifier)),
    Fixes       = nrow(d),
    From        = format(min(ts, na.rm = TRUE), "%Y-%m"),
    To          = format(max(ts, na.rm = TRUE), "%Y-%m")
  )
}

tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(files, summarise_track))
tab <- cbind(Dataset = names(files), tab)
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

---

## 1. African buffalo, Kruger National Park

`data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz`

Six GPS-collared buffalo (*Syncerus caffer*) in Kruger National Park, South
Africa, 2005–2006. Collars reported roughly hourly. This is our workhorse
dataset: several individuals, a long series, a confined landscape with strong
environmental gradients (rivers, vegetation).

::: {.callout-important}
## The lesson this dataset teaches: duplicates

The raw file contains **3,747 rows that duplicate an existing
individual + timestamp combination** — about 13% of the file. These come from
the tag transmitting the same fix more than once. If you compute step lengths
without removing them you get a large number of zero-length steps in zero
elapsed time, and your speed distribution acquires an infinite tail.

We fix this properly in [Session 3](classes/class-03/exercise.qmd).
:::

Used in: Sessions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8.

Source: Getz WM, Fortmann-Roe S, Cross PC, Lyons AJ, Ryan SJ, Wilmers CC.
Movebank study *Kruger African Buffalo, GPS tracking, South Africa*.

---

## 2. Parti-coloured bat, Switzerland

`data/bat_safi.csv.gz`

Seventeen bats (*Vespertilio murinus*) tracked by **VHF radio-telemetry** near
Bern, Switzerland, 2002–2003. Only 1,740 fixes in total.

::: {.callout-important}
## The lesson this dataset teaches: small, irregular, hand-collected data

This is what tracking looked like before GPS, and what it still looks like for
any animal too small to carry a satellite tag. Fixes arrive when a human with
an antenna managed to get a bearing — so intervals are wildly irregular, nights
are dense and days are empty, and individuals have between a handful and a few
hundred locations.

Most of the methods in this course assume regular sampling. Applying them here
without thinking produces confident nonsense — which is exactly why we use this
dataset to practise saying *"no, not with these data"*.
:::

Used in: Session 3 (as a cautionary counter-example).

Source: Safi K, et al. Movebank study *Parti-colored bat Safi Switzerland*.

---

## 3. Turkey vulture "Leo"

`data/vulture_leo.csv.gz`

A single turkey vulture (*Cathartes aura*) called Leo, tracked by GPS for
almost **six years** (2007–2013) between Canada and Venezuela — over 60° of
latitude.

::: {.callout-important}
## The lesson this dataset teaches: one animal, many behaviours

Leo is not doing one thing. He has breeding-ground residency, autumn migration,
wintering residency, and spring migration, repeated over six annual cycles. A
single home range estimate over the whole track is meaningless — it would
describe a "range" covering two continents.

This is the dataset for [Session 4](classes/class-04/slides.qmd): a trajectory
that *demands* segmentation before any other analysis makes sense. It also
crosses many UTM zones, which makes it a good test of whether you have
understood projections.
:::

Used in: Session 4.

Source: Bildstein K, Barber D, Bechard MJ. Movebank study
*Turkey Vulture Acopian Center USA GPS*.

## 4. Environmental rasters for Kruger

All cropped to the buffalo range and stored in `data/`:

| File | What | Resolution | Source |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `kruger_ndvi_2005.tif` | NDVI, two 16-day composites: 2 Feb 2005 (wet) and 14 Sep 2005 (dry) | 250 m | MODIS MOD13Q1, via `MODISTools` |
| `kruger_elevation.tif` | Elevation | ~900 m | SRTM, via `geodata` |
| `kruger_landcover.tif` | Fractional cover of trees, grassland, shrubs, cropland | ~900 m | ESA WorldCover, via `geodata` |
| `kruger_prec_monthly.tif` | Long-term mean precipitation, one layer per month | ~4.6 km | WorldClim 2.1, via `geodata` |

Used in: Sessions 2 and 3. The precipitation climatology is not used in the
practicals; it is there for projects that need a seasonal covariate.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A real scale-factor trap

MODIS stores NDVI as integers multiplied by 10,000, with −3,000 as the fill
value. `MODISTools::mt_to_terra()` already rescales to NDVI units; applying the
0.0001 factor a second time gives values ten thousand times too small. It
happened while this file was being built. Always `summary()` a new covariate
and check that NDVI lies between −1 and 1.
:::

## 5. Fishers in New York (from `amt`)

Four fishers (*Pekania pennanti*) tracked by GPS every 2–15 minutes in New York
State (LaPoint et al. 2013), shipped with the `amt` package together with land
use (GlobCover, 300 m), elevation and human population density.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(amt)
data(amt_fisher)
covariates <- get_amt_fisher_covars()
```

Used in: Session 7.

---

## 6. Mongolian gazelles (from `ctmm`)

Thirty-six gazelles (*Procapra gutturosa*) tracked for about a year, shipped
with `ctmm`. They are **nomadic**: the textbook case of an animal whose
variogram does not level off, so a home range is not a meaningful summary.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ctmm)
data(gazelle)
```

Used in: Session 6.

---

## 7. Simulated animals

`R/simulators.R` contains the random-walk simulators you build in Session 5:
correlated and biased walks, a central-place walker whose true home range is
known (`truth_animal()`, `truth_area()`), and an animal that selects habitat
with a known coefficient (`simulate_ssf()`).

`data/hr_ground_truth.csv` holds the results of `R/hr_ground_truth.R`: twenty
simulated animals, each with five home-range estimates and the true area.

Used in: Sessions 1, 5, 6 and 7.

## Movebank column conventions

Movebank exports share a vocabulary. When R reads the CSV, hyphens in the
header become dots, so `location-long` becomes `location.long`.

| Column | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `event.id` | Unique id of this record |
| `timestamp` | Fix time, **UTC**, `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.sss` |
| `location.long`, `location.lat` | Longitude / latitude, decimal degrees, **WGS84 (EPSG:4326)** |
| `individual.local.identifier` | The animal's name or code — your grouping variable |
| `tag.local.identifier` | The device — *not* the same as the animal |
| `individual.taxon.canonical.name` | Species |
| `sensor.type` | `gps`, `radio-transmitter`, `argos-doppler-shift`, … |
| `visible` | `false` = flagged as bad by the data owner |
| `manually.marked.outlier` | `true` = flagged by hand as an outlier |
| `study.local.timestamp`, `study.timezone` | Local time, if you need day/night |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Two habits worth forming now

**Always keep `timestamp` in UTC** for computation and convert to local time
only for interpretation. Mixing the two is the single most common source of
silent errors in movement analysis.

**Never assume `individual` == `tag`.** Tags get redeployed on different
animals, and animals get recollared. Group by the individual.
:::

## Loading a dataset

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(dplyr)

buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(
    id   = individual.local.identifier,
    t    = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
    x    = location.long,
    y    = location.lat
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE) |>   # the duplicate fix described above
  arrange(id, t)

glimpse(buffalo)
```

## Using your own data

You are welcome to use your own tracking data for the final project. Bring it
in the same shape — one row per fix, with `id`, `t`, `x`, `y` — and tell me
the CRS of the coordinates if they are not longitude/latitude. Talk to me
before Session 5 so we can check the analysis you have in mind is feasible.
